required_hypotheses: a<b and an even number n>=2 of uniform panels; exact-real finite composite Simpson sum.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Input real numbers $a<b$, an integer $n\ge2$, and a real-valued function
$f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ evaluable at every point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the
procedure returns invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. If $a\ge b$ or
$n<2$, the procedure returns invalid-grid. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.

required_hypotheses: Strictly increasing distinct real nodes; the node polynomial, cardinal functions, barycentric weights and finite interpolation sum.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

required_hypotheses: Matching moment data and monic orthogonal polynomial with simple interior zeros; nodes, cardinal weights and rule use that same measure.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

required_hypotheses: a<b, a finite positive Borel measure on [a,b], positive total mass, relative support and the explicitly stated finite moment order.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Fix moment data $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. For an integer $k$ with $0\le k\le m$ and
$2k\le r$, let $V_k=\mathbb R^{k+1}$ with its coordinatewise real vector-space
operations. For $c=(c_0,\ldots,c_k)\in V_k$, let
$P_c(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}c_jx^j$, the evaluation of the formal polynomial with
that coefficient list ([[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]).
Define the **polynomial moment pairing** on $V_k$ by
$$ \langle c,d\rangle_\mu:=\int_{[a,b]}P_c(x)P_d(x)\,d\mu(x). $$
This is a candidate real inner product in the sense of
[[def-inner-product-space]]; its well-definedness and positive definiteness
under the stated support and moment hypotheses are proved in
[[thm-gauss-polynomial-moment-pairing-is-an-inner-product]].

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $m\ge1$ and $r\ge2m-1$. For each
$j=0,\ldots,m$ there is a unique monic real polynomial $p_j$ of degree $j$
such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)q(x)\,d\mu(x)=0 $$
for every real polynomial $q$ of degree less than $j$. For $j=0$, this means
$p_0=1$ and the orthogonality condition is vacuous. The $j=m$ polynomial uses
moments only through degree $2m-1$; its squared norm is asserted only when the
moment datum has order $2m$.

required_hypotheses: Countable Choice, Lebesgue measure on [-1,1], its order-three moments, and the explicit two-node Gaussian rule; exactness through degree three.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and take Lebesgue measure restricted to
the relative Borel sets of $[-1,1]$. Its relative support is all of $[-1,1]$,
so it gives order-three moment data for $m=2$. The moments are
$\mu_0=2$, $\mu_1=0$, $\mu_2=2/3$, and $\mu_3=0$. The monic orthogonal
polynomials through degree two are $p_0=1$, $p_1=X$, and
$p_2=X^2-1/3$. Thus the Gaussian nodes are
$x_1=-1/\sqrt3$ and $x_2=1/\sqrt3$.

The Jacobi matrix is
$$ J_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/\sqrt3\\1/\sqrt3&0\end{pmatrix}. $$
Its unit eigenvectors $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ give weights
$w_1=w_2=\mu_0/2=1$. Therefore
$$ Q_2(f)=f(-1/\sqrt3)+f(1/\sqrt3) $$
is exact for every real polynomial of degree at most three.

required_hypotheses: Continuous f on [-1,1]; definitions of E_n, I_n^L and the Lobatto Lebesgue operator norm, including n=0.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $C[-1,1]$ be the real continuous functions on $[-1,1]$, with
$\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|f(x)|$. Let $\mathcal P_n$ be the
restrictions to $[-1,1]$ of real polynomials of degree at most $n$, including
the zero polynomial. Interval notation is that of [[def-interval]]. Continuity and polynomial degree have the conventions of
[[def-continuity-real]] and
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]].

For each $n\in\mathbb N$ (with naturals in real expressions interpreted by
their canonical real images), the first-kind Chebyshev root angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{R,n}=\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2n+2},\qquad x_j^{R,n}=\cos\theta_j^{R,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They are the roots of $T_{n+1}$ by
[[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]]. For $n\geq1$, the
Chebyshev–Lobatto angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{L,n}=\frac{j\pi}{n},\qquad x_j^{L,n}=\cos\theta_j^{L,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They include both endpoints and are the extrema of $T_n$ by the same
identity. At $n=0$, define the Lobatto node to be $x_0^{L,0}=0$. The
cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, so each listed family has
distinct nodes; the root family at $n=0$ also consists of $0$.

For either family $\sigma\in\{R,L\}$, write its nodes as
$x_0,\ldots,x_n$ and define
$$\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x)= \prod_{\substack{0\leq k\leq n\\k\ne j}} \frac{x-x_k}{x_j-x_k},\qquad I_n^\sigma f=\sum_{j=0}^n f(x_j)\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}.$$
These are the cardinal formula and interpolation sum of
[[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] specialized to this node family.
The displayed cosine arrays decrease, whereas that supplier orders nodes
increasingly: use $z_i=x_{n-i}$ and data $y_i=f(z_i)$. Its cardinal
function with index $n-j$ is exactly the displayed $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma$,
by reindexing the finite product, and its interpolation sum is $I_n^\sigma$.
The empty product at $n=0$ is $1$, so the same identification holds for the
single node. Distinctness makes every denominator nonzero;
[[lem-cardinal-basis-degree-and-values]] supplies the degree and cardinal
values. The finite sum is linear in the data and maps $C[-1,1]$ into
$\mathcal P_n$. Its operator norm is
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma:= \sup\{\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty:g\in C[-1,1],\ \|g\|_\infty\leq1\}.$$
If $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{jk}x^k$, then
$|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|\leq\sum_{k=0}^n|a_{jk}|$ for $|x|\leq1$; hence
$\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty\leq\sum_{j,k}|a_{jk}|<\infty$ whenever
$\|g\|_\infty\leq1$. Define the best degree-$n$ uniform
approximation error by
$$E_n(f):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n}\|f-p\|_\infty .$$

These quantities are real and well-defined. Polynomial functions are
continuous, and sums and scalar multiples of continuous functions remain
continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. The interval
$[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded, so
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] implies
that for every such continuous function $h$ there are finite minimum and
maximum values $m_h,M_h$. Since $m_h\leq h(x)\leq M_h$, one has
$|h(x)|\leq\max(|m_h|,|M_h|)$, so each supremum norm above is finite. The set defining $\Lambda_n^\sigma$ contains
the zero function and is bounded above by the displayed finite coefficient
sum. The set defining $E_n(f)$ contains the zero polynomial and is bounded
below by zero. Completeness of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])
therefore gives the stated finite supremum and infimum. Also, $n+1$ has
positive real image by [[def-canonical-natural]] and
[[lem-of-naturals-positive]], and $n$ has positive real image when $n\geq1$;
thus the root-angle denominator and the Lobatto denominator in its stated
range are nonzero.
